title: DOJ Investigates Nvidia’s $17 Billion Groq Licensing Deal
author: B
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

The US Department of Justice is investigating Nvidia’s $17 billion agreement with artificial-intelligence chip startup Groq, focusing on whether the transaction was structured to avoid the antitrust review applied to an acquisition.

Announced in December 2025, the arrangement gave Nvidia a non-exclusive license to Groq’s inference-chip technology. Nvidia also hired Groq founder Jonathan Ross and other executives. Groq remained an independent company, meaning the agreement was presented as a technology license and recruitment deal rather than a conventional takeover.

According to a New York Times report cited by Reuters, the Justice Department issued Nvidia a formal request for information shortly after the deal was announced. Investigators are examining whether combining a licensing payment with the transfer of key personnel and technology effectively delivered the competitive benefits of an acquisition without triggering the regulatory process.

Groq’s language processing units, or LPUs, are designed for AI inference: the stage when trained models process requests and generate outputs. The company positioned its architecture as an efficient alternative to graphics processors. That makes the competitive question important. Nvidia already dominates AI accelerators, and absorbing a rival’s technology and leadership could reduce independent competition in inference hardware even if Groq continues operating.

An investigation does not establish wrongdoing. No lawsuit or enforcement decision has been announced, and Reuters reported that the transaction is unlikely to be reversed. Consequences could include fines or regulatory action if authorities conclude disclosure or competition rules were violated.

Nvidia said the agreement demonstrates the US innovation system. Groq and the Justice Department did not comment.

The inquiry signals broader regulatory concern about “acqui-hire” transactions, through which dominant technology companies license startup assets and recruit their teams without buying the corporate entity. Its outcome could shape how future AI licensing agreements are reviewed.
